query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy alloys for high‐temperature applications, the ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer is governed by a kinetic balance between element‐specific diffusion rates and redox potentials. Specifically, when the alloy microstructure is refined (i.e., with increased grain boundary density) and the composition is optimized to reduce the concentration of fast‐diffusing elements (e.g., Ti or Mn), the slower but thermodynamically favored oxidation of high redox potential elements (Al and Cr) dominates. This results in the rapid formation of a continuous, adherent, and dense mixed oxide layer (primarily α-Al2O3 and Cr2O3) that effectively limits oxygen ingress.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast high-entropy alloy (HEA) with a coarse-grained, heterogeneous microstructure containing elements such as Al, Cr, Ti, and Mn in near-equiatomic proportion.
generation.intervention: Apply a processing step (e.g., severe plastic deformation or stationary friction processing) to refine the microstructure (increase grain boundary density) and modify the minor element concentrations (reduce fast-diffusing elements like Ti/Mn) while keeping the overall bulk composition similar.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation tests in air at temperatures around 1000–1100 °C for extended durations (≥200 hours) to ensure long-term scale formation and evolution.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased grain boundary density and resultant chemical homogeneity that promotes enhanced diffusional flux of Al and Cr along the boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The refined microstructure enables preferential and enhanced transport of Al and Cr—which have higher redox potentials and form more stable oxides—along grain boundaries. This controlled cation diffusion outpaces the detrimental effects of the more rapidly diffusing species (e.g., Ti, Mn), allowing for the formation and retention of a continuous, dense protective oxide scale. The balanced kinetics restricts oxygen ingress and prevents the formation of porous, non-protective oxides.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to coarse-grained, non-optimized samples, the processed (ultrafine-grained with reduced Ti/Mn content) HEAs will show lower mass gain, thinner and more adherent oxide scales predominantly composed of α-Al2O3 and Cr2O3, and a slower overall oxidation rate.
generation.baseline: HEAs with a coarse-grained microstructure and standard minor element content, which tend to form heterogeneous, thicker, and more porous oxide layers with higher weight gains under identical oxidation conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to high-temperature oxidation in air (≥1000 °C) over long exposures (≥200 hours) for HEAs where Al and Cr are available as primary oxide-forming elements. It may not directly extend to systems dominated by oxidation of elements with very low redox potentials or under oxygen-deficient conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While previous work (PMC6513993::web::015::discussion) shows that reducing Ti content can favor the formation of protective CrTaO4-based oxides, and ultrafine-grained HEAs demonstrate improved oxidation resistance (PMC9026100::web::017::oxidation_kinetics), it remains uncertain how the interplay between grain boundary diffusion and element-specific redox potentials precisely controls the oxide layer’s continuity. This study extends these observations by combining microstructural refinement with minor element optimization—a combination not previously explored in a unified mechanistic study.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples with identical nominal compositions. One set should remain in the as-cast, coarse-grained state, while the other set is processed via a severe plastic deformation method to achieve ultrafine grain sizes and then adjusted to reduce the content of fast-diffusing elements (e.g., by controlled alloying). Subject all samples to isothermal oxidation in air at 1100 °C for 200 hours. Post-oxidation, analyze the oxide scale’s morphology, thickness, phase composition, and overall mass gain using SEM, XRD, and EDS mapping.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and morphology (from cross-sectional SEM)
Phase composition of the oxide (via XRD and EDS mapping)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed, ultrafine-grained, and compositionally optimized HEAs do not exhibit significantly lower mass gains, thinner and more uniform oxide scales predominantly composed of α-Al2O3 and Cr2O3, or if no marked improvement in oxidation resistance is observed relative to the coarse-grained baseline, the proposed mechanistic hypothesis is falsified.

Complex multi-element alloys are gaining prominence for structural applications, supplementing steels, and superalloys. Understanding the impact of each element on alloy surfaces due to oxidation is vital in maintaining material integrity. This study investigates oxidation mechanisms in these alloys using a model five-element equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy, in a controlled oxygen environment. The oxidation-induced surface changes correlate with each element’s interactive tendencies with the environment, guided by thermodynamics. Initial oxidation stages follow atomic size and redox potential, with the latter becoming dominant over time, causing composition inversion. The study employs in-situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure techniques to elucidate the oxidation process and surface oxide structure evolution. Our findings deconvolute the mechanism for compositional and structural changes in the oxide film and will pave the way for a predictive design of complex alloys with improved resistance to oxidation under extreme conditions. Moreover, the sub-surface oxidation and porosity caused by the Mn diffusion toward the oxide layer were completely suppressed from 10 at.% of Al, reducing the overall thickness of the oxide layer from ≈25 μm (Mn15Al5) down to ≈1 μm. Considering the above-stated, changing the content of Al can be used for precise tailoring of the complex performance of the prepared alloys to achieve desired properties not only at the laboratory but also at elevated temperatures.
